Axial loading and structures

    13Axial loading and deformation

    When a bar is subjected to an axial load, deformation occurs. Combining σ = P/A with Hooke's law gives the single most used formula in the unit.

    PA = E δLL  ⟹  δL = PLAE13.1

    Read it as a stiffness statement: the member behaves like a spring of stiffness AE/L. Doubling the length doubles the stretch; doubling the area halves it. The product AE is called the axial rigidity.

    The four standard cases

    Every axial problem in this unit reduces to one of four arrangements. In all of them the governing idea is the same — divide the bar into segments within which P, A and E are all constant, apply 13.1 to each, and add the results algebraically (extensions positive, contractions negative).

    One axial load, different cross-sections. The internal force is the same P in every segment; only the area changes.

    δl = Pl₁A₁E + Pl₂A₂E + Pl₃A₃E

    Several axial loads, uniform cross-section. The area is constant but the internal force changes at every point of load application. Cut each segment, draw its free body, and find the force it actually carries — this is the step most often got wrong.

    δl = P₁l₁AE + P₂l₂AE + P₃l₃AE

    The method, in one line

    Make a cut in the segment of interest, keep one side, and sum the external forces on that side. That sum is the internal force for that segment. Never use the largest applied load for the whole bar.

    Different loads and different sections together. Nothing new — segment the bar wherever either the load or the area changes, then sum.

    δl = Σ PiliAiE

    Uniformly tapered circular bar. The area now varies continuously, so the sum becomes an integral. Take an element of thickness dy at distance y, where the diameter has grown linearly from d₁ to d₂, and integrate over the length.

    δl = 4PLπEd₁d₂13.2

    Note the neat result: the tapered bar behaves exactly like a uniform bar whose diameter is the geometric mean √(d₁d₂) of the two ends, not the arithmetic mean. Setting d₁ = d₂ recovers eq. 13.1 as it must.

    Prismatic and stepped bars. Enter the internal force carried by each segment — not the applied load — along with its length and area. Tension positive.

    Tapered bar calculator

    14Types of structures

    There are two types of structure, classified by the number of unknowns relative to the number of available equilibrium equations.

    Statically determinate structures

    If the structure can be solved using the static equilibrium equations alone — ΣV = 0, ΣH = 0, ΣM = 0 — it is statically determinate. Three equations, three unknown reactions. The internal forces depend only on geometry and loading, never on the material, so a steel truss and an aluminium truss of identical geometry carry identical member forces.

    Statically indeterminate structures

    If the structure cannot be solved by the equilibrium equations alone, it is statically indeterminate. There are more unknowns than equations, and the shortfall — the degree of indeterminacy — is the number of extra relations needed. Those extra relations are compatibility equations, statements about how the deformations must fit together, and they are used alongside the equilibrium equations to solve the structure.

    The three-step method

    1. Equilibrium. Write ΣH = 0 (or ΣV = 0) relating the unknown reactions to the applied loads.
    2. Compatibility. State the geometric fact that closes the problem. For a bar fixed at both ends, the total change in length is zero: δ₁ + δ₂ + δ₃ = 0. For a bar with a gap, the total change equals the gap.
    3. Substitute. Express each δ as PL/AE and solve the two equations together.

    The consequence engineers care about

    In an indeterminate structure the load distribution depends on the relative stiffness of the members: the stiffer path attracts more load. This is exploited deliberately in airframes — a stiff spar cap draws load away from a skin panel — and it is also why a badly shimmed joint can be overloaded without any change in the external loads.

    15Worked problems

    Ten problems covering elastic constants, axial deformation, and statically indeterminate members. Attempt each one before opening the solution.

    Problem 1Elastic constantsSolution included

    A concrete cylinder of diameter 150 mm and length 300 mm, when subjected to an axial compressive load of 240 kN, showed an increase in diameter of 0.127 mm and a decrease in length of 0.28 mm. Compute (a) Poisson's ratio, (b) the modulus of elasticity, (c) the modulus of rigidity and (d) the bulk modulus.

    Read the answer critically

    The measured data give ν = 0.907. Section 09 showed that no real isotropic material can exceed ν = 0.5, and the consequence appears immediately in step (d): K comes out negative. Work the arithmetic exactly as shown for the method marks, then state that the result is physically inadmissible — the quoted diameter change is too large for a concrete cylinder under this load. Recognising this is worth more than the answer itself.

    Show the worked solution
    Problem 2Triaxial stress and volume changeSolution included

    A concrete bar 300 mm long with a uniform 30 mm × 50 mm section is acted on by the following forces over their respective cross-sections: 25 kN along the length (tensile), 350 kN across the width (compressive) and 200 kN through the thickness (tensile). Take E = 140 GN/m² and Poisson's ratio 0.25. Determine the change in volume, length, width and thickness.

    Show the worked solution

    16Formula sheet

    Everything in Unit I on one screen. Print this page to take it into a revision session.

    QuantityRelationNotes
    Normal stressσ = P/AP normal to A; N/mm² = MPa
    Shear stressτ = P/AP parallel to A; halve for double shear
    Normal strainε = δL/LDimensionless
    Shear strainγ = τ/GIn radians
    Hooke's lawσ = EεValid within the elastic limit only
    Poisson's ratioν = lateral / linear strain0 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5
    Volumetric strainεV = εx + εy + εz= δV/V
    Bulk modulusK = σ/εVHydrostatic loading
    Relation AE = 2G(1 + ν)Forces E/3 ≤ G ≤ E/2
    Relation BE = 3K(1 − 2ν)K → ∞ as ν → 0.5
    Relation CE = 9GK / (3K + G)ν eliminated
    Axial elongationδL = PL/AEPer segment; sum algebraically
    Tapered barδL = 4PL / (πEd₁d₂)Geometric mean diameter
    Triaxial strainεx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)] / ETension positive
    Indeterminate barΣF = 0 with Σδ = 0Equilibrium + compatibility
